articles.title: World’s smallest country plans an 80MW solar plant on land; nearly 10 times larger than Vatican City in a $117 million project
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Vatican City occupies only about 44 hectares, making it the smallest independent state in the world. Its population is around 800 people, with thousan.
articles.body: Vatican City occupies only about 44 hectares, making it the smallest independent state in the world. Its population is around 800 people, with thousands more travelling into the territory each day to work. Yet the tiny state is preparing for an energy project on a very different scale. The Vatican plans to invest about €100 million, or $117 million, in an agrivoltaic plant intended to supply its electricity needs and move it towards carbon neutrality. The facility will not be built inside Vatican City itself. Instead, solar generation is planned for a much larger piece of Vatican-owned land outside Rome, where the project is expected to take between 18 and 24 months to complete.The Vatican is smaller than its planned solar site outside RomeThe Vatican's territory is simply too small for the planned installation. As reported by Fortune, the solar and agricultural project is being developed at the Santa Maria di Galeria estate, a Vatican-owned property roughly 1,050 to 1,100 acres in size outside Rome.The difference between the two sites is striking. Vatican City covers about 109 acres, while the estate where the new facility is planned is close to ten times larger. The project is expected to provide between 80 and 90 megawatts of generating capacity.The plant is not being designed for a major industrial operation or a huge computing campus. It is intended to meet the energy requirements of the Vatican, including electricity used by its buildings and a radio transmitter.The scale of the land also makes for an unusual comparison with the rapidly expanding data centre industry. A site of similar acreage is being used for OpenAI's Stargate project in Abilene, Texas, where the planned infrastructure is intended to support around 1.2 gigawatts of AI computing capacity.The Vatican's proposed installation would generate a fraction of that amount. Its purpose is very different.From 2,394 rooftop panels to an 80MW solar projectThis would not be the Vatican's first move into solar power. In 2008, 2,394 solar panels were installed on the roof of the Paul VI Audience Hall. That system produces around 300 megawatt-hours of electricity each year.The new facility would represent a substantial expansion of that existing capacity. Its planned 80 to 90 megawatts would be several hundred times greater than the capacity represented by the audience hall installation.The project is also intended to combine energy generation with agricultural use, rather than simply covering the estate with conventional solar infrastructure. That approach is reflected in the term agrivoltaic, which describes systems where solar generation and agricultural activity share the same land.For the Vatican, the project is part of a longer climate programme rather than an isolated investment.The plan began under Pope FrancisThe roots of the project go back to Pope Francis. In June 2024, he formally set out the Vatican's plans in a letter known as “Fratello Sole”. Pope Leo XIV has continued the project since becoming pope. He visited the Santa Maria di Galeria site in June 2025 and described the development as a significant opportunity. Italy agreed to the project the following month.The institutional arrangements then took further shape. In June 2026, the Vatican formalised its relationship with Italian utility company ACEA, with both sides involved in developing the renewable-energy facility.The latest step is the financial commitment. Around €100 million has now been attached to the project, giving a clearer indication of the scale of the investment. As reported by Reuters, construction is expected to take between 18 and 24 months.A small country with a much larger energy comparisonVatican City's physical size makes comparisons with modern infrastructure particularly striking. The country is roughly one-eighth the area of New York's Central Park. Its population is only around 800 residents, while close to 3,000 lay workers commute into the Vatican.That makes its electricity requirements tiny compared with those of the enormous data centres now being planned across the United States. Some individual AI facilities are expected to require electricity on a scale comparable with that used by tens of thousands of households or an entire small city.The Hyperion data centre project in Louisiana, for example, is expected to draw as much as 5 gigawatts of power by 2030. Against that figure, the Vatican's planned 80 to 90 megawatts is modest.The comparison is useful for another reason. Both projects involve large amounts of land and electricity infrastructure, but they are being built for completely different purposes. One supports intensive computing operations. The other is intended to power a small sovereign state.The wider pressure on electricity suppliesThe Vatican's project comes as electricity demand from data centres is rising sharply. Data centres accounted for roughly half of new US electricity demand in 2025, according to figures cited by Fortune. Global data centre electricity consumption is also projected to more than double by 2030, reaching about 945 terawatt-hours.The growth is beginning to influence the wider power industry. Utilities are planning major investments to accommodate additional demand, particularly in areas where clusters of AI data centres are being developed.The comparison with the Vatican is therefore less about the absolute amount of electricity involved and more about the very different scales of modern energy demand. The Vatican's planned plant is large relative to what the state currently generates, but small beside the facilities being built to supply the computing industry.A carbon-neutral goal by 2050The Vatican has already committed itself to reducing emissions. Its 2023 climate pledge to the United Nations set a target of cutting emissions by 20% from 2011 levels by 2030, alongside a longer-term goal of reaching zero emissions by 2050. The renewable-energy project is intended to help with that transition.The climate position of the Catholic Church became particularly prominent during Francis's papacy. His 2015 encyclical, Laudato Si', addressed environmental protection and climate change as issues with moral as well as scientific dimensions. It also argued that wealthier countries carry a greater share of responsibility for greenhouse-gas emissions.Leo XIV has maintained a similar position. During a United Nations climate conference in 2026, he called for urgent action on climate change and referred to creation as “crying out”.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Former ‘Alligator Alcatraz’ detainee says he was placed in phone booth-sized cage for 15 hours
articles.summary: For around 15 hours, immigration detention officers kept Raúl Suárez Herrero confined in a cage slightly larger than a phone booth, where he feared snakes and endured mosquitoes in the middle of Florida swampland, the former detainee alleged.
articles.body: For around 15 hours, immigration detention officers kept Raúl Suárez Herrero confined in a cage slightly larger than a phone booth, where he feared snakes and endured mosquitoes in the middle of Florida swampland, the former detainee alleged. Suárez, 59, told José Díaz-Balart in an interview for Noticias Telemundo’s “Ahora 360” that he was forced into the cage, measuring 7 feet, 9 inches high and 4 feet, 3 inches square, for praying out loud for an ill young man at “Alligator Alcatraz,” an ICE detention site. “I feel like I was in hell,” Suárez later told NBC News in a phone interview from Mexico, where he was deported. Suárez spoke days after a Department of Homeland Security watchdog confirmed the use of the phone booth-sized cages at the now-shuttered Florida detention camp in a Sept. 11 report. “The use of such restrictive spaces is highly unconventional and does not align with standards for humane treatment,” the report said. The DHS Office of Inspector General report documented its inspectors’ findings during an unannounced January visit to the Ochopee, Florida, site. In December, Amnesty International issued its own report on conditions at the detention site based on interviews with detainees and its own tour of the facility. The organization detailed the use of the small cages and said it amounted to torture. The facility staff told inspectors that the cages were “calming areas” where immigrants could de-escalate and have time alone and that no one spent more than two hours inside them. But Suárez told Noticias Telemundo that “they took me there and I spent more than 15 hours inside in that little hole,” referring to the small cage. He said he was forced in around 1 p.m. and taken out at about 5 a.m. “when morning was breaking.” According to Suárez, the cage was in a recreation area where detainees took exercise time. Suárez said he couldn’t stretch out on the cage floor and got little sleep for fear of what might slither into the cage. “I had to be careful because on the ground there were snakes and you don’t see them. You can’t fall asleep because they can come into the cage,” Suárez said in a video interview. DHS did not directly address Suárez’s allegations or case in response to questions from NBC News. But a spokesperson rejected “claims that there were ‘inhumane’ conditions” at the immigrant detention center. Those claims are “categorically false” and any allegations of excessive use of force are “FALSE,” the spokesperson said in an email. “No detainees were being beaten or abused,” the DHS spokesperson said. DHS provides long-standing medical, dental and mental health services, three meals a day that are evaluated by certified dietitians, clean water, clothing, bedding and hygiene products and access to phones to talk with family and lawyers, the spokesperson stated. Alligator Alcatraz’s standards were consistent with those under other administrations, the spokesperson also said. Further questions were referred to the state of Florida, “as this facility was managed by the State of Florida through the Division of Emergency Management.” The facility in the heart of the Everglades was built by Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis as part of the state’s push to support President Donald Trump’s aggressive immigration crackdown. Alex Lafranconi, a spokesman for DeSantis, has dismissed criticism of the small cages. Lafranconi has described the small cages as a confinement area for “violent criminal aliens who have proven they cannot remain peaceful,” and said “we’d make them smaller, if we could.” Although DHS said the inspector general “indicated” all recommendations have been administratively closed, the OIG said in its report that the administration did not address its 10 recommendations, including that it “discontinue the use of the small metal enclosures to hold detainees for any reason or amount of time.” The OIG also said that at the time of the inspection, all the detainees were ICE detainees and there was evidence that ICE had some degree of oversight authority and engagement at the facility. Originally from Cuba and in the U.S. since he was 12, Suárez was detained by ICE in July 2025 during an ICE check-in. Before it was recently ordered closed, Alligator Alcatraz had been denounced by multiple detainees and legal and immigrant advocates for its conditions. The detention facility’s records state the average time people were placed in the smaller cages with metal fencing was 59 minutes and 27 seconds, according to the OIG report. But the OIG said it could not confirm or refute ICE officials’ assertions regarding use of the enclosures or detainees’ allegations they had been denied food or other abuses. The small cages at the facility were supposed to be a “safe and secure place” where people could “reflect on their behavior choices, manage their emotions, reduce stress, and practice self-directed behavior,” according to the detention camp’s policies, the report stated. According to detention center records cited by the OIG, 79 people were held in the small cages during the period of July 17, 2025, to Jan. 18, and none were held more than two hours. Detainees in the small cage “may leave at any time by detainee request or per staff directive,” according to the report. But Suárez was adamant that his confinement was not voluntary and lasted far more than two hours. “Everybody lied” about the small cages, Suárez said, disputing that he could have gotten out or requested to be let out. He said he was forced into the cage after praying out loud for a man who had an epileptic seizure as they were waiting to get registered at the detention camp. Help for the man was taking “too long,” according to Suárez. That’s when he said he started praying aloud, as he used to do at the evangelical church he attended before his arrest. “I asked God for the young man’s life,” he said. Suárez alleged two guards then forced him to stand up, asked where he was from and then grabbed him and dragged him “all the way back to where that little cell was.” He said he was kicked in the leg so hard he thought they broke it. “My leg was so big and black.” “They just dropped me over there and locked the doors,” he said. He said he got no medical treatment for his leg or a medical evaluation after the confinement. Suárez said his experience has left him psychologically “shattered.” Suárez was removed to Mexico in February after more than four decades of living in the United States. He was detained on July 16, 2025, when he went to an immigration check-in. Suárez had been ordered removed from the U.S. in 2000 after serving a prison sentence stemming from a plea agreement on a drug charge. Because Cuba was not accepting U.S. deportees then, Suárez was released and told to check in with ICE annually, a court document states. Cuba has allowed few of its citizens to return after U.S. deportation. An attorney attempted to get Suárez released from detention. The federal judge had given DHS until late January to remove him or release him, but the judge then extended the government’s time for two weeks. On the deadline date, Feb. 11, DHS deported Suárez to Mexico and the judge closed the case. “Forty-seven years. They took me to the U.S. as a 12-year-old, when I was a child,” Suárez said. “I was raised my whole life there [in the U.S.]. I’m bilingual and everything. I went to school there and everything. And everything happened from one moment to the next. I still can’t absorb what happened.” Suárez said he had been a truck driver since he was 17 and had built his own truck driving business with his brother, an American citizen, who died in 2021 from Covid. His father had died in Cuba when he was 3 and his mother, who became a U.S. citizen, died about a decade ago. When immigration laws were toughened in 1996, making legal residents deportable for certain crimes, he could no longer seek U.S. citizenship, he said. His mother had urged him to get citizenship, but he didn’t do it, he said. “I was pretty young. When you are pretty young, you don’t listen to anybody,” he said. He had no other encounters with law enforcement, he said. He said he’d been living a normal life, preparing to buy a house and had a girlfriend. “Life is changed. I don’t know what is going to happen here in Mexico.”

articles.title: Healey to ask EU finance ministers to let UK into industry scheme
articles.summary: The chancellor wants the Made in Europe programme to deepen ties with the UK "rather than erecting new barriers".
articles.body:
The chancellor is to warn the European Union (EU) not to lock the UK out of its scheme to protect industries from unfair Chinese competition.

John Healey will push for closer UK-EU partnerships on tech, defence, and manufacturing at a meeting of EU finance ministers in Dublin on Friday.

But he will call on the EU to design its "Made in Europe" programme in a way that deepens ties with the UK "rather than erecting new barriers", Treasury sources told the BBC.

Officials said Healey will tell European finance ministers it is important to "learn lessons" after talks collapsed last year for Britain to join an EU defence loans scheme.

That dispute centred on how much money the UK would pay to join.

The "Made in Europe" policy, officially called the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), is currently being considered by the bloc and aims to protect EU manufacturing with restrictions on goods from outside countries.

There is concern in government the scheme could lock British firms out of European supply chains.

Treasury officials said Healey wanted to reduce the economic impact of Brexit and build closer ties with the EU, but not at any cost to the UK.

Healey said: "The next chapter of Britain's growth story will be written in more places.

"To me, closer ties with the EU means British businesses – wherever they are based across the UK – get better access to both the supply chains and the customers they need to grow."

Healey will use the meeting in Dublin to focus on tech firms, defence companies, and manufacturing.

"The chancellor wants to make sure nothing holds them back," a Treasury source said.

It comes after a reset summit with the EU was delayed after Sir Keir Starmer's resignation as prime minister.

Treasury sources now expect that to take place in November.

Healey's meeting in Dublin comes after it emerged earlier this week that he is in discussions about joining a global investment bank aimed at raising more money for defence spending.

He is considering a bid to join the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank (DSRB), not long after his predecessor Rachel Reeves rejected the idea.

Canada has been leading efforts to establish the bank, which supporters say would enable governments to borrow at lower costs to increase military spending.

Paying for the UK's growing defence commitments is one of Healey's biggest headaches as he prepares for the Budget in October and next year's spending review.

articles.summary: Meyer Lansky II reveals personal letters and memories of his mob boss grandfather in a new book exploring the infamous organized crime figure's legacy.
articles.body: To Prohibition-era gangsters, history buffs and true crime aficionados, he was Meyer Lansky, the financial mastermind who built an international gambling empire. To his namesake, he was simply "grandpa." Meyer Lansky II, the grandson of the late mob boss who helped establish organized crime across the nation, reflects on his grandfather through personal letters, photographs and firsthand memories in his new book with S. J. Peddie, "The Lansky Legacy: The Life and Letters of Meyer Lansky." "He never mentioned the names of anybody that he worked with. He was always cautious with that," Lansky told Fox News Digital. CHARLES MANSON'S GRANDDAUGHTER REVEALS MOMENT SHE DISCOVERED DARK FAMILY SECRET: 'IT WAS DEVASTATING' Growing up in Washington state, the younger Lansky initially saw his grandfather as a stern, serious figure who strictly compartmentalized his life. The elder Lansky never brought up his underworld dealings; instead, he focused on teaching his grandson how to present himself to the world, introducing him to fine details like tie pins and shoehorns. "Growing up in Washington state, I wasn't exposed to those kinds of things anywhere else," Lansky said. "He was always asking me about my grades, my studies and what books I was reading. "He’d give me basic advice: ‘Whatever you do, do a good job. Be honest with people, provide good service and people will come back to you.’" SAMMY 'THE BULL' REVEALS WHY HIS LOVE FOR JOHN GOTTI TURNED INTO PRISON HATE The elder Lansky, widely dubbed the "mob's accountant," rose to prominence in the early 20th century alongside childhood friends Benjamin "Bugsy" Siegel and Charles "Lucky" Luciano. Together, they revolutionized organized crime, building lucrative gambling operations from Havana to Las Vegas. "He was right alongside Luciano and Bugsy Siegel during the transformation of the syndicate into the modern American Mafia," Lansky said. That reputation carried real-world danger. The younger Lansky recalled a chilling incident from his childhood, when his grandfather's notoriety and perceived wealth nearly led to his kidnapping. As he grew older, the veil began to slip. EX-MOB CAPO ALLEGES FURIOUS RFK WEAPONIZED THE FBI AGAINST HIS FATHER OVER MARILYN MONROE "One day I was listening to the radio and heard that Treasury Secretary John Connally was going to Las Vegas to investigate Meyer Lansky," he said, referencing the decades-long, unsuccessful federal effort to convict his grandfather. "When my grandfather visited a week later, I told him, ‘Hey, I heard your name on the radio.’ He looked at me, smiled, and said, ‘You did?’ He didn't elaborate, but I knew at that point he realized I was going to figure out who he really was." EX-COLOMBO CRIME FAMILY CAPO REVEALS HOW GAS TAX SCHEME RAKED IN MILLIONS OF DOLLARS WEEKLY While mob historians contend that the Polish-born gangster perfected modern money laundering and amassed vast fortunes, a central mystery remains: What happened to the money? If the elder Lansky stashed away millions, his grandson noted, the family never saw it. Yet, the physical legacy remains impossible to ignore. articles.title: The New Yorker claims women can be 'kind of pregnant' in article questioning pregnancy tests
articles.summary: The New Yorker faced backlash for promoting an essay claiming a woman could be "kind of pregnant," sparking debate over pregnancy as a biological state.
articles.body: The New Yorker drew criticism Thursday after promoting an essay that described the binary distinction between being pregnant and not pregnant as "misleading" and said a woman could be "kind of pregnant" or "a little bit pregnant." The essay, "The Unsettling Ambiguity of Early Pregnancy," by Apoorva Tadepalli, examined the uncertainty surrounding early pregnancy tests, miscarriage and viability through the writer's experience with multiple pregnancy losses and her current pregnancy. The magazine promoted the piece on X by saying at-home tests capture only a moment when an embryo has implanted and that someone could be "kind of pregnant, a little bit pregnant, or almost pregnant, or maybe pregnant" while still testing positive. MED SCHOOL DEANS COME UP EMPTY IN TENSE HEARING WHEN ASKED POINT BLANK IF MEN CAN HAVE BABIES: 'RIDICULOUS' Los Angeles County Republican Party Chair Roxanne Hoge, a mother of four, told Fox News Digital that uncertainty over whether a pregnancy will remain viable does not change whether a woman is pregnant. "As a mother of four and an actual biological woman, I must applaud the author for noticing that women do, in fact, make babies," she said. "While I sympathize with her on the very sad reality of carrying a pregnancy after a loss, this was a lot of words to try and pretend that a fetus is a clump of cells. You're either pregnant or you're not." Elizabeth Barcohana, America First Policy Institute California ambassador to the America First Women's initiative, said the distinction should be between the existence of a pregnancy and whether a woman knows that pregnancy is viable. "A woman cannot be ‘a little bit pregnant.’ Pregnancy is a physical, biological state that begins when a fertilized embryo implants in the uterus and triggers a chemical hormonal reaction," Barcohana said Thursday in a statement to Fox News Digital. "This article is not about being pregnant. It is about a woman’s experience about knowing whether she is carrying a viable healthy pregnancy." Tadepalli described testing positive during five pregnancies and spending periods of those pregnancies unsure whether she would miscarry. She said those experiences affected her ability to emotionally embrace her current pregnancy, with much of the essay examining what early testing can and cannot tell women about what will happen next. PRO-LIFE PUBLISHER FACING DEMANDS TO RETRACT CALLING ABORTION ‘KILLING’ FIRES BACK: ‘THE ANSWER IS NO’ Lisa Cusack, president of the Don’t L.A. My Burbank PAC, told Fox News Digital she viewed the article’s framing as an attempt to make pregnancy more subjective while arguing that uncertainty in early testing does not change whether a woman is pregnant. "This article just seems like a tortured attempt to make pregnancy into a subject experience in order to justify abortion," she said. "The fact that an at-home pregnancy isn’t sophisticated enough to pick up the beginning stages of every pregnancy doesn’t mean you’re ‘kind of pregnant,’ or that pregnancy itself, which literally begins with conception and ends with birth, is ‘nonlinear.’ "Women have always known that early pregnancies sometimes don’t take or show up on tests, but that doesn’t change the fact that you’re either pregnant or not, whether you know it or not or want it or not." WHAT MY SON'S ULTRASOUND TAUGHT ME ABOUT ABORTION — AND MASSACHUSETTS IGNORES Barcohana said that element of the essay was relatable to women who have experienced pregnancy loss and blamed The New Yorker’s presentation for shifting attention away from it. "The New Yorker’s editors betrayed the author with this provocative headline, because what she’s really talking about — in a vulnerable way that millions of women can empathize with — is the utility and impact on women of unreliable early testing," she said. "She tried to talk about something totally legitimate for women trying to start a family, and they [editors] hijacked it." Fox News Digital reached out to The New Yorker for comment but did not immediately receive a response. The distinction between detecting pregnancy and determining whether it is viable is also reflected in medical guidance. The Food and Drug Administration says at-home pregnancy tests detect human chorionic gonadotropin, or hCG, a hormone produced after a fertilized egg is attached to the uterine wall. The agency notes that testing too early can produce inaccurate results and that a positive home test does not provide information about how a pregnancy will develop. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists states that pregnancy begins when a fertilized egg is implanted in the uterus, while pregnancy viability can require additional evaluation as development progresses.

articles.title: SC raps CBSE for refusing to exempt Class VI from 3-language policy this year
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court on Thursday rapped CBSE for being stubborn in its decision to enforce the three-language policy from this year for Class VI s.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Supreme Court on Thursday rapped CBSE for being stubborn in its decision to enforce the three-language policy from this year for Class VI students and forced it to reconsider the decision with a clear mandate, camouflaged as a suggestion, to enforce it from next academic year.CBSE had decided to enforce the three-language policy for all classes from Class VI to X, in which the students were to choose three languages of which two must be indigenous. On SC's request, it reconsidered and agreed to enforce it from Class VI onwards from this year while students in Class VII to X were to be governed by the old policy.SC had asked CBSE to reconsider exempting students of Class VI this year.A bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana is dealing with a bunch of petitions challenging the threelanguage policy, including highlighting the inadequacy of textbooks, indigenous subject teachers and infrastructure.When additional solicitor general Aishwarya Bhati told the bench that CBSE is disinclined to exempt Class VI this year and argued, “Let the Class VI students start this year as they would have three more years before appearing in Class X board examination,” the bench said, “It is your cohort who decided that it must be enforced from Class VI without considering the comfort of the Class VI students upon whom you sprung a surprise.”“When the notification for enforcing the policy came, the student was already in Class VI. Go back and reconsider. Anyway, the academic year will come to an end in a few months. You enforce it for Class VI students from the 2027-28 academic year,” it said.Bhati agreed to take back the decision for reconsideration. The bench said exempting Class VI students from the policy this year would be without prejudice to CBSE’s right to defend the policy. “The exemption is purely from the aspect of logistics and balance of convenience,” it said.SC said, “There are more contentious issues on what can be considered an indigenous language (Petitioners say English should be considered as one while Centre objects to it) which we will decide later.”It added, “There must be some degree of comfort for the students. Those who would be coming to Class VI next year would know in advance that they must choose languages as per the three-language policy.You can also make it optional for Class VI students with adequate incentives so those who want to conform to the policy can choose to do so.” SC posted the matter for further hearing on Wednesday.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Trinidad and Tobago ends state of emergency amid pushback over mass arrests
articles.summary: Lawyers criticised mass arrests under emergency powers that allowed authorities to detain people without charge.
articles.body:
The Caribbean country of Trinidad and Tobago has ended a state of emergency that granted the government extraordinary powers to combat crime, including the ability to imprison people without charge.

The country’s prime minister told parliament on Wednesday that the government would not extend the state of emergency. One was issued in 2024 and another in 2025, with extensions lengthening both. Instead, the government would seek a “permanent legal framework”.

“The proposed legislation will establish a permanent legal framework for targeted operations against violent crime, gangs, illegal weapons and the criminal networks that finance them, while providing safeguards for law-abiding citizens, judicial oversight and parliamentary accountability,” Prime Minister Kamla Persad-Bissessar said in a social media post.

The government had faced criticism for a campaign of mass arrests that suspended key civil liberties in what it said was in the name of cracking down on crime and those the government deemed threats to security. A prominent businessman and his wife were among those arrested over alleged involvement in a plot to assassinate the prime minister, but were never charged and later released.

The measures were last extended in June, with the prime minister stating that more than 5,800 people have been arrested since a March extension. About 2,250 of those have yet to be charged, and it remains to be seen whether they will be released now that the state of emergency has ended.

Lawyer Criston Williams told The Associated Press news agency that he expects some of those detained without charge to bring lawsuits against the government and called for the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights to investigate possible abuses by the government.

“They are transported to us blindfolded, shackled, hands behind their backs, a gray knapsack over their heads,” he said, adding that meetings with lawyers took place in the presence of five armed men from law enforcement, “who refer to themselves as operator one, two, three, four, five. There’s a camera above, so guess what, there’s nothing like attorney-client privilege.”

Police reported a record 624 killings in the country of about 1.4 million people in 2024, a figure that police say dropped to 369 in 2025. Police state that 255 killings have been recorded this year, compared with 268 over the same period in 2025.

articles.title: Robotics: Firms race to improve robot training systems
articles.summary: Training systems that allow robots to negotiate the real world are getting more sophisticated.
articles.body:
Freddo the robot walks across the office and takes a plastic bottled offered by a staff member.

Given that a robot recently beat Usain Bolt's 100m sprint record, it's not the most startling achievement.

But the speed by which Freddo has been trained to walk, recognise the bottle and grasp it is impressive. It took just a few minutes to develop those skills and upload them to Freddo. His developers say rival systems could take days to attain such skills.

I'm at Vsim, a British start-up based in Cambridge. Founders Michelle Lu and Kier Storey hope one day their software will control robots that can navigate and do useful tasks in the home and workplace.

"It's a weird situation with robotics because actually the stuff that we find as humans to be incredibly difficult, like gymnastics, you can get robots to do reasonably well. The stuff that humans are really good at, like fine dexterity, is really hard in robots," Storey says.

Freddo's skills were honed in a virtual environment, where a task can be performed in a computer simulation millions of times. Once the optimum solution (known as a policy) is found, it can be uploaded and used by the hardware - in this case Freddo.

Such virtual simulations are a common way to train robots. Tech giant Nvidia has a system called Isaac Sim which works that way - Lu and Storey both worked on an early version of it.

In 2022 they decided to set up Vsim, to build the their own training system environment and other tools.

As they were starting from scratch Lu and Storey could optimise the software to exploit the powerful computer chips used in AI, known as graphics processing units or GPUs.

"The underlying algorithms that we were using for most of these robotic simulations they hark back to the 1970s and 1980s, but those algorithms are not really brilliant fits for GPUs," Storey says.

Within months they realised their system could work much faster than anything they had seen before.

"Eighteen months in and we actually have a completely functional, super high-performance simulator," says Lu.

The software is so efficient that it can run on the hardware carried by Freddo. That means the robot can run tens of thousand of simulations while it is moving around.

"It can look about a second, or so, ahead into the future for 20,000 different kind of combinations of things that might happen," Storey explains.

And that would be vital for a robot moving around an unstructured environment like the average home.

"Things outside of the robot's control, like humans, animals or even other robots, could do things that require a change of strategy. These unexpected events could happen very quickly and the robot needs to be able to quickly adapt to ensure its actions remain safe and on-mission," Lu says.

Vsim is a start-up with 10 engineers working on its tech. Nvidia is at the other end of the industry. It dominates the market for computer chips used for AI and has a leading robotics software division, with hundreds of engineers.

It does not build robots, instead it has a suite of software designed to let organisations train and control robots.

That includes virtual simulation training systems and a so-called world model , called Cosmos, which gives a robot an understanding of the physics of the real world and how its environment might change as it moves around.

But even with the powerful computer resources available to Nvidia, the software only gives a rudimentary understanding of the real world.

"Manipulation, - where I just grab a bottle, that's not too hard. The problem is when you start doing long-horizon tasks, where I say: 'I want you to take the bottle and I want you to fill it up and I want you to go pour'," says Spencer Huang, director of product for robotics at Nvidia.

But he's confident that good progress is being made. This year Nvidia has started using AI agents to help build virtual environments to train robots and validate whether the solutions from training work or not.

"When we talk about creating the [virtual] world and actually scanning it in - a lot of that is actually manual labour.

"We're just throwing agents at it... it's basically given us a huge workforce," Huang says.

Simulation is not the only method for training robots. They can also be trained by watching human or video demonstrations.

Rika Antonova has been working in the field of robotics since 2015 and is currently an associate professor at the Department of Computer Science and Technology at the University of Cambridge.

Her research is focused on developing software and hardware that can aid robots to learn complex behaviour.

Antonova works with a training system called MuJoCo, owned by Google's DeepMind since 2021. It's open-source software, which means researchers can use it for free, and are allowed to tinker with the code.

"It is very, very user-friendly. So for research groups or for small start-ups, that's useful," she says.

She says that Vsim's approach - very fast simulation - is promising.

"If you have a very, very fast simulator, then you can simulate hundreds of millions of samples in that few seconds that your robot is thinking about how to adjust its motion, and then you can change the motion almost in real time," she says.

But those simulated environments are still rough approximations of the real world, which limits what can be trained.

"There are certain things that are hard to model in simulation, like highly deformable objects and cutting," she says.

It's a challenge that Nvidia and Lu and Storey at Vsim are working on.

Lu says their system has "reduced approximation, using accurate simulations to train models that genuinely work in reality as well as they do in simulations."

Soon a second robot, to be called Nacho, will be helping develop that tech.

Lu says that should speed up their development process and ensure their software can run on different machines.

And, of course, provide Freddo with some company.

articles.title: Why we bought our first home with a 100% mortgage - despite the risks
articles.summary: The share of UK mortgages with smaller deposits is the highest it's been since 2008. The BBC spoke to borrowers about how they manage the risks.
articles.body:
Until last year, Conroy, 32, and his partner Amber, 28, saw little prospect of owning their own home. They were renting in central Manchester where they work and could not afford to save up for a deposit.

Then they came across a relatively niche, and some experts say riskier, type of mortgage that offered a solution.

The Track Record mortgage from Skipton Building Society covers 100% of the value of a property, with the borrower paying nothing upfront.

Borrowers must meet strict eligibility checks and pay a higher interest rate - in Conroy and Amber's case 5.33% fixed for five years - but they were happy to do this. And in August they bought a four-bed home for £242,000 in Swinton on the edge of Manchester.

"I don't think it's dawned on us it's really ours," says Conroy, a video editor.

According to the Bank of England, the share of UK mortgages with deposits worth less than 10% of the property's value is currently the highest it has been since 2008 when such loans were widely available.

The average deposit for first-time buyers is currently around 20%.

It comes as lenders such as Lloyds, Santander, Skipton and Yorkshire Building Society have launched a raft of new mortgage deals over the last few years covering upwards of 95% of the value of a property, and in some cases as much as 100%.

They say they want to help first-time buyers get on the housing ladder as property prices continue to rise and while saving for a deposit remains a struggle.

But these loans tend to charge higher rates, aren't available for all types of property or borrower, and come with risks customers should be aware of.

Conroy and Amber, a solicitor, have a 25-year loan with monthly repayments of £1,500 - roughly what they were paying in rent.

He says they feel comfortable with the higher cost because they "earn quite well" and expect their salaries to rise.

But he is aware there is a greater risk of falling into negative equity with a no- or low-deposit mortgage. That is when the value of a property falls below the value of the loan still owed on it - leaving the borrower with potentially painful costs if they suddenly have to sell.

Conroy says they plan to overpay their mortgage for the first five years to build up more equity in their home.

"There is always the element of a gamble with the property market," he says.

"But I have researched the area we moved to and don't think house prices are going to drop."

Twenty-seven-year-old Bronya and her partner George, 29, also used a low-deposit mortgage to buy their four-bedroom house in Rhuddlan, North Wales in August.

Lloyds lent them £258,000 - roughly 98% of the property's value - over a 33-year term and they only had to put down £5,000 as a deposit.

The couple pay an interest rate of 5.89%, fixed for five years, equating to monthly repayments of £1,400 - about the same as what they paid to rent a one-bed flat before.

Bronya, a civil servant, says they could have put down a bigger deposit but wanted to use their savings for a renovation project costing upwards of £20,000.

They are aware of the risks of negative equity but believe the refurbishment will boost the value of their home.

"We also plan to stay here our whole lives," George adds, explaining that they are prepared to ride out any dips in the property market.

Widespread uptake of low-deposit mortgages by borrowers who could not afford them was seen as a major factor in the 2008 global financial crisis.

But today's deals have much stronger affordability checks and do not pose the same risks, says David Hollingworth, associate director at brokers L&C Mortgages.

Borrowers of Skipton's zero-deposit mortgage, for example, have to prove they have kept up with their rent for at least 12 consecutive months and credit payments for the last six months.

And Lloyds won't issue one of its £5,000 deposit mortgages for new-build properties and shared ownership homes.

Hollingworth says lenders are recognising that some people have "good affordability but may be struggling to save for a deposit while paying a rent and dealing with cost of living pressures".

Following a recent rule change, he adds, lenders are also offering more "flex" on how much someone can borrow as long as it's within their means.

Nevertheless, he urges borrowers to use common sense.

"Think carefully - what do monthly payments look like? Are you aware that interest rates could go up?"

articles.title: India's hospital boom is improving access but pricing millions out of critical care
articles.summary: Indian hospitals have attracted billions in funding, but the gap between public and private care is widening.
articles.body:
On a recent visit to Miraj, a small town in western India where I grew up, I counted more than 50 multi-specialty hospitals, diagnostics centres and health clinics packed along a five kilometre stretch of road.

Many of them had come up in just the past five years, even though the town has historically been a regional medical hub in the state of Maharashtra.

The proliferation of these new facilities tells the story of the unprecedented boom in India's private healthcare industry over recent years.

Hospitals have been undertaking breakneck expansion every quarter by adding thousands of new beds, diagnostics chains are expanding their footprint across smaller towns and medical institutes are raising hundreds of millions of dollars through the public markets to expand presence across the country.

In early August, Manipal Health, India's largest multi-specialty hospital, raked in nearly a billion dollars in what became India's second largest initial public offering (IPO) this year.

The sector has also been a darling of global private equity (PE) investors. Between 2022 and 2024, Indian healthcare and pharma companies recorded nearly 600 mergers and acquisitions and private equity transactions valued at more than $30bn.

Forty per cent of these funds went to hospitals, according to data from Grant Thornton.

An additional amount over $20bn was raised by the sector in the last two years, as per more recent data obtained from the consultancy by the BBC.

Yet, even as the country's health infrastructure has seen a radical improvement in access as a result of this investment wave, millions of Indians have been priced out by the boom.

This was borne out by a new report released by a government panel recently, which highlights the strikingly unequal nature of India's burgeoning healthcare economy, raising serious concerns about a "deepening affordability crisis" in the country's private hospitals.

The report found that treatment in private hospitals is often between five and 10 times costlier than in government facilities, with the gap further widening for serious illnesses such as cancer, heart disease and kidney failure.

It also said the "unbridled" growth of clinics, nursing homes and diagnostic centres and uneven implementation of regulatory standards had led to "glaring disparities in both the quality and cost of care in private sector, leaving patients vulnerable to arbitrary pricing and substandard practices".

It further blamed "rampant commercialisation of private healthcare" for increased patient grievances when it came to things such as excessive billing, unnecessary diagnostics, and soaring costs for routine procedures like childbirth, which it said was "directly pushing vulnerable households into catastrophic debt and distress, causing asset sales".

Earlier this week, the food and drug regulator in India's richest state, Maharashtra, also found IV (intravenous) sets being sold at an astonishing profit margin of 2,800% in hospitals, raising concerns over the pricing of medical devices, which it said was almost entirely unmonitored .

The government panel had a range of recommendations to address the challenges: among the more contentious of them, a cap on hospital room tariffs to the nearest three-star hotel level, price regulation of essential treatments, diagnostics, and routine procedures across all private hospitals and standard treatment guidelines to prevent over-treatment. It also red-flagged foreign ownership of over 51% in hospital chains.

India's private hospitals have pushed back against some of the proposals.

In a statement to the BBC, Siddhartha Bhattacharya, Secretary General of NATHEALTH, an association representing India's private healthcare sector, said the government should focus on reducing structural costs of healthcare delivery including taxes, land, capital, manpower and regulatory compliance requirements - rather than capping rates.

According to him, healthcare delivery is capital-intensive and investment-heavy and return on capital employed "hovers at around 10%, significantly lower than many other sectors of the economy, which often generate 1.5-2.5 times higher returns on capital".

He also cautioned against comparing hospital tariffs with hotel tariffs, saying it overlooks key compliance requirements that hospitals have to adhere to, such as infection control standards and patient safety norms, all of which add up to costs.

The country's biggest hospital chains, from Max Healthcare to Fortis, have warned that such arbitrary caps will " stifle " investment into the sector and scare away foreign investors if they are unable to get risk-free returns on their money.

But public health experts say there is definitely a need to debate price regulation, given that private healthcare in India is currently entirely a seller's market.

"With big foreign private equity money coming in, especially in tertiary care, it is people outside the country who are basically making decisions on price points. That should not be the case," Dr Srinath Reddy of the Public Health Foundation of India told the BBC.

Government intervention is all the more critical given the "super profits" many of these hospitals have been making, said Vivek ND, another health policy expert.

"The increased emphasis of these hospitals on conducting various tests, pushing for diagnostics which might not be required must also be looked into," he said.

Some of the proposals - such as a fairer goods and services taxation regime which the panel recommends - could be welcome steps to reduce the cost of private health care, according to Vivek, though he adds wider consultations with the industry are required before any recommendations are made binding.

Dr Reddy agrees. Before the government arbitrarily decides price caps, proper countrywide estimates on the precise cost of private healthcare are needed, he said.

"Costs will differ state to state and city by city, so you can't impose blanket caps across the country," he said.

But as this debate heats up, the broader thrust, experts say, must be on strengthening public healthcare to reduce patient costs, something which even the panel recommends.

India's current government health expenditure at 1.4% of gross domestic product (GDP) has been below the 2.5% target set in the National Health Policy almost a decade ago, and much behind the 5% prescribed by the World Health Organization.

The govenrment panel's report itself notes that disproportionately low spending on secondary and tertiary healthcare has driven citizens towards expensive private facilities, resulting in "catastrophic out-of-pocket expenditure".

The government will "have to up its game" with more public investment to reduce the common man's dependence on private hospitals, said Vivek.

But at the same time, the reality is that India needs an estimated $300bn in additional healthcare investment to build capacity.

A big chunk of that capital will evidently come from private domestic and foreign investors, leaving policymakers with the task of ensuring that investors don't flee even as ordinary people aren't priced out of essential services.

articles.title: Driver charged with 2nd-degree murder in L.A. bus crash that news helicopter was covering
articles.summary: Officials say Bailee Lynn Rios was intoxicated and driving against traffic when she slammed into a city bus. A news helicopter covering the deadly incident also crashed, killing three people.
articles.body: LOS ANGELES — The woman accused of ramming into a Los Angeles city bus Tuesday has been charged with second-degree murder in the deadly crash, officials announced Thursday. Bailee Lynn Rios, 36, was arrested Wednesday in connection with the crash, which killed two passengers. While it was covering the tragedy, a news helicopter crashed nearby, killing the reporter and the pilot on board and a pedestrian on the ground. “What is particularly tragic about this case is that this is a preventable tragedy,” Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman told reporters. In addition to the two counts of second-degree murder, Rios has also been charged with driving under the influence of a drug and reckless driving, according to a complaint. “She will be looking at a maximum sentence of life in prison,” Hochman said. It was not immediately clear whether Rios had an attorney who could speak on her behalf. According to police, Rios drove her 2004 Ford Expedition the wrong way down a busy street, ran a red light and hit a car before she slammed into the bus. She was rescued by first responders and taken to a local hospital. Investigators found drugs in Rios’ car following the wreck, and prosecutors suspect she was driving under the influence, Hochman said. “She was driving well beyond the speed limit, she entered into opposing traffic because she was approaching a red light where cars were stopped, and she didn’t stop,” he said. One passenger was fully ejected from the bus and another was partially ejected, police said. Video from the scene in Chatsworth, a neighborhood in Los Angeles’ San Fernando Valley, showed Rios’ SUV partially wedged into the middle of the bus. In a helicopter high above, reporter Eliana Moreno described the crash as “horrific” on live television. “This is terrifying,” she said in what would become one of her final broadcasts. Moreno and pilot George Marciniw were killed when the chopper, providing coverage for NBC Los Angeles and Telemundo 52, suddenly lost altitude and plummeted toward two storage containers. A person on the ground, Edy Gutierrez Mejia, also died. NewsChopper 4 was owned and operated by Angel City Air. The deaths left Chatsworth and the greater Los Angeles community in shock and mourning. Rios’ loved ones said they never could have imagined she would be involved in something so horrific. “It’s so awful,” her mother, Cindy Rios, told NBC News in a brief phone call Thursday. Rios’ longtime friend Brad Aragon told the California Post that Rios had struggled with addiction in the past and went to rehab at least once. He confirmed the Post’s reporting to NBC News. On social media, Rios occasionally posted about being in recovery and battling addictions. Friends left encouraging words and offered help if she needed it. Hours before the crash, Aragon and Rios had texted each other about planning a visit in October. She seemed shaken by recent events in her life and said she was hanging around with people she knew were toxic, Aragon told the Post. According to court records, Rios was convicted in 2022 of driving with a suspended license. Previous charges of driving under the influence, drug possession and carrying drug paraphernalia were dismissed. Hochman said his office is still examining her criminal record. Rios is expected to be arraigned Friday, he said. She is being held on $4 million bail. Asked whether the three helicopter-related deaths would be rolled into Rios’ case, Hochman declined to speculate. “We’ll wait to see what the investigation reveals, and then we’ll make the call at that time,” he said.

articles.title: Spotted wildcat from Bolivian forest revealed as new species
articles.summary: A spotted wildcat long mistaken for relatives has been identified as a new species in Bolivia.
articles.body:
A spotted cat from the forests of Bolivia has been confirmed as a new species.

The small feline, about the size of a domestic moggy, went under the radar because it was confused with other wild cats that share similar spots and stripes.

But DNA studies show the cat is actually in a class of its own, highlighting how much remains unknown about some of the world's most elusive mammals.

Scientists hope the discovery will draw attention to the conservation of tiger cats, a group of small wild cats found in South and Central America that receives far less public attention than their larger cousins like lions, leopards and tigers.

Tiger cats are small, spotted wild cats found across Central and South America, from Costa Rica to Bolivia and Argentina.

They look remarkably similar and even experts can struggle to tell them apart.

"It's an amazing result that we have a new species for the world, which is the Leopardus tilcayo ," said Paola Nogales-Ascarrunz of Universidad Mayor de San Andres in La Paz, Bolivia.

"It's amazing that there are still new species waiting to be discovered: we don't have to go to a volcano, an island, or deep into the sea."

Only one confirmed member of the species is known - a cat living in a rescue sanctuary in Bolivia - but scientists believe others exist.

It was this 10-year-old cat, nicknamed 'Tigrino', that set scientists on the path to discovery.

Bolivian scientist Dr Nogales-Ascarrunz was volunteering at the sanctuary when she noticed the cat looked unusual.

It had been found in the forest by a local resident, who initially thought it was a domestic kitten. As it grew older, however, it became clear that it did not behave like a house cat.

Dr Nogales-Ascarrunz had heard of other sightings of small wild cats in the dense forests of the country's Yungas region, but these had not been investigated by scientists.

To solve the mystery, she joined forces with other researchers from around the world to investigate the family history of tiger cats, using DNA from living animals and museum specimens.

"There's so few records or pictures, no individual in a museum, so it was hiding because nobody was looking," said Eduardo Eizirik, a conservation geneticist at the Pontifical Catholic University of Rio Grande do Sul in Brazil.

The study, published in Current Biology , uncovered further surprises, suggesting there are five rather than three tiger cat species, including the newly described Tilcaya cat ( Leopardus tilcayo ) of Bolivia.

However, identifying the species is only the first step.

Co-researcher Dr Caroline Sartor, of the Wildlife Conservation Research Unit at the University of Oxford, said the discovery was important for conservation because it is impossible to protect a species if we don't know what it is or where it lives.

"These are animals similar in size to a domestic cat, so you might think we would know them all by now, but this discovery shows how much biodiversity is still to be uncovered in some of the less-studied regions of the world," she said.

Tiger cat species are considered vulnerable to extinction because of deforestation, habitat loss and illegal hunting, although the new species is missing from previous assessments.

The discovery could also have wider implications for the world's cat family.

Both wild and domestic cats belong to the biological family Felidae, which includes every living cat species from tiny house pets to massive tigers.

There are officially 41 species recognised but the new discovery, and the finding that there may be several species of tiger cat, brings the number to 44 or more.

Andrew Kitchener, an expert in mammals at National Museums, Scotland, who was not involved with the research, says the small spotted South American cats known as tiger cats have been a "taxonomic nightmare".

"These cats are confusing because they look so similar and there are few specimens in museums, so even now we are still learning how to tell them apart as genetics reveal more species," he said.

articles.title: US approves $414M uranium investment in Niger, two years after troops left
articles.summary: Uranium project investment could mark a turning point in US-Niger and US-Canada relations.
articles.body:
The United States government has signed off on as much as $414m in financing for a uranium project in Niger, according to the project’s developer, two years after Washington agreed to withdraw troops from the African country.

The US Development Finance Corp approved the debt facility for Canadian miner Global Atomic’s Dasa project, which the company describes as the highest-grade uranium deposit in Africa, according to a company statement on Wednesday.

The investment could bolster US access to a strategic uranium supply at a time when Niger, the world’s seventh-largest uranium producer, is locked in a dispute with French state-backed miner Orano, which long dominated the country’s uranium sector.

Sources briefed on the effort said US Ambassador Kathleen FitzGibbon had urged Washington to rebuild ties with Niger and back the project after the Trump administration took office with a renewed emphasis on deal-making in Africa.

In 2024, the United States agreed to withdraw about 1,000 troops after the military government, which took control of Niger in a coup in 2023, deemed their presence “illegal” and turned to Russia for security support. French soldiers were also ordered to leave in 2023.

The project was seen as an opportunity to secure access to a strategic energy resource that might otherwise fall into the orbit of rival powers, the sources said.

One source familiar with discussions involving Global Atomic and the Development Finance Corp said a breakthrough came this summer when chief executive Stephen Roman travelled to Washington to resolve remaining issues holding up approval.

The project could also provide a rare bright spot in US-Canada relations, which have come under strain amid a trade war between the neighbours.

Niger’s government did not respond to Reuters’ request for comment.

The project faces significant security and political risks.

Last month, a group of soldiers launched attacks on a key military airbase, the presidential palace and other sensitive sites in the capital, Niamey, in an attempted mutiny, authorities said.

Niger later accused France of orchestrating the offensive, which it denied.

Global Atomic has been exploring alternative routes to export uranium from the landlocked country due to the security risks, a source briefed on discussions said.

One idea has been to invest in a route north through Algeria and across the Sahara Desert.

Algeria sent aircraft to Niger last month to help the government respond to the attempted coup, indicating strengthening ties between the neighbouring countries.

Uranium was added to the US critical minerals list last year, prompting renewed interest in Niger’s reserves.

articles.title: Dangote refinery: Share-buying frenzy makes oil barons out of Nigerians
articles.summary: Many Nigerians buy their first ever shares - in the oil refinery owned by Africa's richest man, Aliko Dangote.
articles.body:
At least that is what the social media memes would have you believe as investor fever hits the country.

Nigerians have been eager to have a piece of the energy business that was built up by the country's – and continent's – richest man: Aliko Dangote.

More than four billion shares in his giant oil refinery – representing just over 3% of the company - went on the market on Monday in Africa's biggest-ever sale of its kind.

The minimum purchase was 10 shares for about $4 (£3) and despite this only representing a miniscule portion of the firm, many are now celebrating and joking about their new-found (part-)owner status.

One popular social media video has a Nigerian narrating how he stopped a speeding Dangote company lorry driver, telling him not to be reckless with company property.

Other memes show investors trying to phone up Dangote to discuss business matters.

And the term "Yangote" – a pun in the Hausa language essentially meaning "we all have a share now" - has been trending on social media.

On the first day of the Initial Public Offering (IPO), investment apps crashed as they could not handle the high demand.

Bamboo, which runs one of the most popular investor tools here, later apologised, saying: "We know we let you down."

Public affairs analyst Jamil Ubah said he had rarely seen Nigerians as excited about something as this. He argued that it fed the dream that it could lead to greater riches for a population that is often battling to make ends meet.

"I think the hope for the common man is that his money will grow into something big, and don't forget this is coming at a time when many are struggling as the economy is not doing great," he told the BBC.

Dangote wanted this to be "the people's IPO" with drivers, cooks, cleaners and servants having the chance to be part of something big.

Twenty-five-year-old clothes seller Idris Lawal Musa made his first-ever stock exchange purchase and told the BBC he was happy after investing 21,000 naira ($16; £12) in 40 shares.

"It is no longer Dangote but 'Yangote', the company belongs to us now," he said while laughing.

"I am a trader by profession and when I see that the shares have increased in price I will sell," he noted.

The popularity also reflects a growing investment culture among younger Nigerians who have embraced mobile trading platforms, cryptocurrencies and digital savings products.

But fear of missing out may have also pushed some to get into the investment business.

In the build-up to the IPO, social media platforms were awash with financial conversations. People shared subscription guides, debated valuation metrics and encouraged friends and family to participate.

But amid the frenzy, experts have warned that there are risks – shares can go down in value, as well as up, meaning people could lose some, or all, of their investment.

Financial analyst Shuaib Uwais said prospective investors should avoid thinking of the IPO as a guaranteed route to wealth.

He urged people to consider a number of factors that could impact the refinery's future performance, including disruptions to crude oil supply, operational challenges, regulatory changes and fluctuations in demand for refined petroleum products.

"If for any reason the company experiences difficulty in sourcing its raw materials, there could be challenges," he told the BBC.

Nevertheless, the IPO has given people the chance to be part of this home-grown success story.

Dangote's sprawling refinery on the outskirts of Lagos, which began operating two years ago and now processes around 700,000 barrels of crude a day, has transformed the fortunes of Nigeria's oil sector.

Until recently, Africa's largest crude oil producer had no refining capacity and had to import the finished product. Now the Dangote refinery is feeding much of the domestic demand.

But for Dangote, the share offer is about raising cash to fund the growth of the business, something that the country's mini-magnates may now be able to get behind.

articles.title: Australia cracks down on student and backpacker visas to curb migration
articles.summary: Rest of World News: SYDNEY: Australia will stop foreign students from bringing partners and children to accompany them while they study and tighten working holiday visa r.
articles.body: SYDNEY: Australia will stop foreign students from bringing partners and children to accompany them while they study and tighten working holiday visa rules, a senior minister said on Thursday, amid growing debate over high migration levels.The government's move comes after the hard-right One Nation party, which has been surging in recent polls, said this week that it would slash the number of temporary migrants by 750,000 over three years, to give Australians "breathing space."Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke dismissed suggestions the changes were politically motivated by the One Nation party, which describes its approach as "Australia first" and whose policies have drawn comparisons to those of U.S. President Donald Trump."It's simply demonstrably wrong to suspect that somehow this is a recent bit of work done to deal with a political climate - it's not," Burke told reporters.The reforms are expected to bring annual net migration down to about 225,000 by 2028 - broadly in line with pre-pandemic levels - from around 300,000 now. The cost of living and immigration have consistently ranked among voters' top concerns in recent polls.Ballot for backpackersUnder the new measures, a ballot system will be introduced for backpackers seeking to extend their working holiday visas. All visitor visas will carry a "no further stay" provision preventing holders from remaining in Australia while applying for another visa category such as a partner visa.International students will only be permitted to renew their student visas if they move up the qualification scale.Some students from Pacific Island nations and Southeast Asia will be able to bring their partners and children, but secondary applicants will not be allowed on most student visas.Spouses and partners of international students can currently work in Australia, although the number of hours they are permitted varies depending on the course of study.International education contributed A$53.6 billion ($38 billion) to the Australian economy in the year to June 2025, making it the country's fourth-largest export. Despite this, foreign students have been a central focus of the centre-left Labor government's migration reduction efforts.Student visa application fees have risen by nearly 300% to A$2,500 over the past four years, while English-language requirements and minimum savings thresholds for graduate visa applicants have also been tightened.Migration surged after Australia reopened its borders in February 2022 following nearly two years of COVID-19 closures, driven largely by international students, backpackers and temporary workers.However, numbers have been declining over the past two years. Net overseas migration stood at 306,000 in the year to June 30, 2025, with international students accounting for more than half, down from a peak of 518,000 in 2023.($1 = 1.4085 Australian dollars)Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: Independent Nebraska U.S. Senate candidate Dan Osborn appeared to confirm leaked audio in which he suggested Trump supporters' lives are "suck so f---ing bad."
articles.body: Independent Nebraska U.S. Senate candidate Dan Osborn appeared to confirm leaked audio on Wednesday in which he suggested people who supported President Donald Trump have lives that "suck so f---ing bad." In audio obtained by The Omaha World-Herald, Osborn seemed to be heard demeaning Trump supporters in Nebraska, claiming they only support the president because he's "on the winning team." "Billy Bob in f---ing Red Cloud, Nebraska, who lives next door to the f---ing Trump store as you pull into town and is waving the Trump flag … all he knows is he’s like on the winning team," the speaker who appeared to be Osborn said. "He’s been so effective at taking Billy Bob and his wife Mary Jane or Mary Jo and telling them, ‘Look, we’re winning. You’re on the winning team.’ And that’s all they care about because their lives probably suck so f---ing bad." FOUR MONTHS TO MIDTERMS: 12 RACES THAT WILL DETERMINE THE SENATE MAJORITY When asked about the audio on CNN's "Inside Politics with Dana Bash," Osborn said, "It sure sounds like me," but added that it sounded "out of character" for him. "I talked to a tremendous amount of people and, again, I don’t remember the context of this one particular conversation, but it certainly does sound out of character for myself," Osborn said. "I’ve always lived by the golden rule — treat others like you want to be treated — and if somebody was offended by this, certainly I would apologize to those people that might be offended, but I got to tell them I feel their pain. I absolutely feel the pain. We’re all angry right now, and sometimes when you’re angry you say some things." During the interview, Osborn emphasized that the audio was not what he truly thought of Trump voters and instead a discussion on the "disenfranchised" voters. FOX NEWS POLL: 'RESILIENT DISCONTENT' DEFINES THE US MOOD AT 250TH ANNIVERSARY "I talked to a lot of Trump voters and … I’m talking about people are pissed off, people are disenfranchised, especially, and that’s what Trump captured in Nebraska. He captured people who are angry about the political system, and Trump ran outside of that as an outsider," he said. "That’s what people like about Trump. It’s why I’m running again as an independent running outside the political system because I’m tired of the two-party doom loop." Fox News Digital reached out to Osborn's campaign for comment but did not immediately receive a response. Osborn's opponent, incumbent Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., told Fox News Digital, "I've been to Red Cloud. I've been to every corner of Nebraska. The people Dan Osborn is mocking are the hardest-working people in America. They don't need a candidate who looks down on them. They need a senator who fights for them. That's what I do every day." JASMINE CROCKETT DISPARAGES MAGA VOTERS, TRUMP AS 'MOST UNPATRIOTIC PEOPLE' Earlier this month, Fox News Digital obtained audio of Osborn suggesting he would appeal to Republican voters by distancing himself from progressive issues. "The state is made up of 50% Republicans, 26% Democrat, 24% independents. So my win numbers, mathematically, I have to get probably 10-15% of Republicans to win this race. How am I going to do that by f---ing saying, ‘Oh, I love trans people, and they should be able to play in sports?’" Osborn said. "F--- no, Jane, that’s not how I win. I win by s---ing on the party." In another clip, he was heard saying, "I have people recording me, so I can’t say I want to abolish ICE. I can’t say those words. I’ll be f---ed." Osborn has also predominantly supported other Democrats' campaigns.

articles.title: Meet Lillie: The 7-year-old British student who copied a puffer fish's trick to design a jacket that can puff up
articles.summary: Europe News: A 7-year-old British student has seen her ocean-inspired idea move from a child’s drawing towards a real prototype. Lillie’s Puffy Coat was one of fou.
articles.body: A 7-year-old British student has seen her ocean-inspired idea move from a child’s drawing towards a real prototype. Lillie’s Puffy Coat was one of four inventions selected from hundreds of entries in the Little Inventors programme, supported by Dogger Bank Wind Farm and South Tyneside Council. Inspired by the way a puffer fish expands when threatened, the jacket is designed to puff up and help its wearer feel safer, braver and more confident. According to Dogger Bank’s report, local businesses are now working with the young inventors to turn their ideas into physical creations.7-year-old Lillie turned a puffer fish trick into a jacketLillie’s idea began with a piece of inspiration from the ocean. She looked at the puffer fish and its ability to puff itself up, then imagined how a similar idea could be used in clothing.Her invention, named the Puffy Coat, was designed to expand around the wearer. The purpose was not simply to make an unusual-looking jacket, but to create something that could help a person feel safer and more confident.The concept stood out among hundreds of ideas submitted to the Little Inventors programme. Four inventions were eventually chosen for development into physical prototypes. Lillie’s Puffy Coat was one of them, alongside Isla’s Crabey 3000, Dexter’s 5G Power Paddle and 11-year-old Oliver’s Magni-Sub.For a 7-year-old, having an idea selected was only the beginning. The next stage was to work with people who could explore how the drawing might actually become something that could be built.Local businesses helped turn the drawing into a prototypeThe Puffy Coat is being developed with support from Ford Aerospace, while the physical prototype is being created by Orbital FX, a North East creative fabrication specialist. Orbital FX is also working on Isla’s Crabey 3000 and Dexter’s 5G Power Paddle.The programme arranged initial design visits so the children and their families could meet the teams responsible for developing their inventions. Instead of simply handing the drawings over to adults, the young inventors were involved in discussions about their ideas and how they might work in the real world.Luke Daley from Orbital FX helped lead these sessions. The meetings gave Lillie and the other children an opportunity to ask questions, explain their thinking and explore what might be possible when a simple drawing is turned into a physical object.What did Lillie think about seeing her idea take shapeLillie was able to show the team her invention and discuss how she thought it could work. She was particularly excited about seeing what the Puffy Coat would look like once the prototype was finished.The experience was designed to be hands-on rather than purely theoretical. The children could talk directly with the people helping to develop their ideas and see how their concepts were being considered as real designs.For Lillie, that meant the puffer fish-inspired coat had moved beyond an idea on paper to a collaborative project.The project connects children with real-world innovationThe Puffy Coat is part of a wider programme intended to show children that their ideas can have a life beyond the classroom. Dogger Bank Wind Farm and South Tyneside Council have supported the Little Inventors programme since 2022, with a focus on STEM education and encouraging young people to explore creativity, innovation and future opportunities.The programme draws inspiration from the Dogger Bank wind farm being built off the North East coast. According to Dogger Bank, the partnership has helped thousands of local schoolchildren explore subjects including renewable energy, climate action and innovation.These projects give children a chance to see how creative ideas can be developed with help from people who work with design, engineering and fabrication.When will Lillie’s Puffy Coat be unveiledThe next major milestone for Lillie and the other young inventors will come in 2027. Dogger Bank reports that all 4 prototypes will be unveiled in a public exhibition at The Word in South Shields, England. The exhibition will bring together Lillie’s Puffy Coat, Isla’s Crabey 3000, Dexter’s 5G Power Paddle and Oliver’s Magni-Sub. It will mark the point at which the children’s original ideas can be seen as physical prototypes.For Lillie, the journey from noticing a puffer fish to designing a jacket inspired by its defensive behaviour shows how a simple observation can spark an inventive idea.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
