articles.title: Afghan female medical students fear being sent home from Pakistan
articles.summary: Afghan medical students are in despair as they fear being deported from Pakistan
articles.body:
Nooria, which is not her real name, still remembers one of the moments that made her want to be a doctor.

It was back home in a village in Afghanistan, where she was born. A 13-year-old boy there became sick and died because of appendicitis.

"He was completely healthy, but the road was blocked and he died on the way. There are multiple incidents just like this."

"That and the potential I saw in myself, I thought I can be a doctor for them, I can help."

She fears that dream could now be over and that she could be sent back to Afghanistan. That would be the end of any chance at a career for Nooria who, as a woman, is barred from studying or working by Afghanistan's Taliban government.

Earlier this month, Pakistan's Medical and Dental Council - the medical education regulator - issued a letter to all medical and dental colleges across the country saying that students from Afghanistan studying in their colleges must return to their home country. Failure to follow the directive, it said, would be "viewed seriously" and may lead to regulatory action. A temporary stay order from the Lahore High Court stopped students in Punjab, such as Nooria, from being deported immediately until the next hearing, scheduled for Friday. There is no certainty that the stay will continue.

Since 2023, hundreds of thousands of Afghans have been deported from Pakistan and over two million have left according to the UN. These numbers increased as the relationship between Pakistan and Afghanistan dramatically deteriorated in the last year. Pakistan has accused Afghanistan's Taliban government of harbouring militant groups, which it denies.

The announcement from the medical council was met with a strong reaction. Amnesty International called the decision "patently discriminatory and arbitrary" and said that "Pakistan has obligations under international human rights law to uphold the right to education without discrimination on the basis of national origin." Several of Pakistan's former envoys to Afghanistan also urged the council to reconsider; one called it "shocking" and "a question of humanity, compassion and Pakistan's own moral responsibility".

The council told the BBC that they can give no further comment while the court case continues, but their lawyer has told the BBC that none of the Afghan students were registered with PMDC. The students say that this is the responsibility of their colleges, not them; a notification issued by the PMDC earlier this year directs colleges to ensure that students are registered.

The medical and dental students the BBC has spoken to say they do not see how the relationship between the two countries should affect their ability to study.

For Nooria, this stings even more because she says it took a lot for her to get here. She first began studying at Kabul University, but as the Taliban forces approached the city, she left. She was offered what she thought at the time was a lifeline: the opportunity to study medicine in Pakistan on a scholarship. Now a final year student at a medical university in Lahore, she says she has given everything to the course.

"I was studying, day and night. I couldn't sleep because there was so much pressure and knowledge that I had accumulated in my mind. I got used to it a bit, but I have compromised a lot. My relationships, talking to my family, spending time with my friends. I think I haven't lived for these years, I have only studied for my dream."

So when she heard about the letter, Nooria was in shock. She's still nervous about the repercussions of speaking out, which is why she asked we don't reveal her name.

"We knocked on every door, our teachers, organisations, anyone we thought could help us. We are under so much pressure that we have completely forgotten about our studies, we don't know what will happen to us."

Final year students like Nooria have their last exams in just a few months. Said Mubin, another final year student in Punjab, is in the same position.

"I was in complete despair, my mind was blank. It was like a panic situation because they were giving us very short time to evacuate the (accommodation), the college," he says.

Other students have also brought cases across the country, but different directives have been issued, adding to the confusion. Some students told the BBC that they have finished their exams but not completed the practical training - known as a 'House Job' - to complete their medical education.

Without completing their degrees, both Mubin, Nooria and many other medical and dental students the BBC spoke to, fear that none of their credits will be recognised by another institution.

"It means you have to start from zero, from your first year," Mubin says.

Both Nooria and Mubin have valid student visas, seen by the BBC. The PMDC did not provide the BBC with the number of students they believe are affected, but Anayatullah Momand, a spokesperson for the Afghan medical students, has said that they estimate it's approximately 1,000 medical and dental students, 65% of whom have visa holders. Some are still waiting for a visa, but Momand said that 15% have had their visas cancelled or have not yet applied for one.

While the medical council's letter makes no distinction between students with the right documents, Pakistan's Ministry for Foreign Affair's spokesman did. "Our policy is that those Afghan students who are in Pakistan on a valid visa and registered for a valid course will continue and complete his or her education," said Sajjad Haider Khan during a recorded press conference at the ministry.

Similar comments were made the previous week, but the students say they have not seen any change to their situation.

With the outcome of her studies still uncertain, Nooria has been trying not to think about what returning to Afghanistan could mean.

"My family counted on me. These five years I have sacrificed everything that would be zero, multiplied by zero. And then I would become a poor and helpless Afghan female, facing this destiny. I cannot imagine this."

articles.title: Finnish foreign ministry official details how Russia's 'hybrid warfare' reshaped border security
articles.summary: Finland built 124 miles of border fencing after Russia allegedly weaponized migration as hybrid warfare against the Nordic NATO member state.
articles.body: Russian tactics designed to disrupt European nations forced neighboring Finland to fundamentally rethink its border security, culminating in the recent completion of a new border fence along its eastern frontier. Finland constructed roughly 124 miles of fencing along its border with Russia — a secondary security measure intended to stem the flow of unauthorized Russian migrants, Petri Hakkarainen, political director for the Finnish Ministry for Foreign Affairs, told Fox News Digital. "We have in the past witnessed Russia's attempts… to instrumentalize migrants at the Finnish border," Hakkarainen said. "Basically pushing migrants towards our borders, forcing us then to take them on." NATO ALLY POLAND WARNS RUSSIA, BELARUS PUSHING ILLEGAL MIGRANTS TOWARD ALLIANCE — AND THE US A sudden influx forces the Finnish government to process large volumes of asylum claims, which could destabilize society if carried out on a massive scale, he explained. In response, Finland closed its entire land border with Russia in 2023. Moscow swiftly filed a formal complaint, condemning the closure as "Russophobic." The Kremlin expressed "deep regret" over the move, claiming it replaced decades of "pragmatic, mutually respectful relations" with an anti-Russian political stance. Finland shares an 833-mile border with Russia — the longest of any European Union or NATO member state. The completed border fence supplements the border closures. As Russia remains locked in a war of attrition in Ukraine, Western officials have accused Moscow of launching widespread destabilization campaigns, ranging from disinformation to state-sponsored economic coercion intended to erode public trust across Europe. FINLAND’S FOREIGN MINISTER SAYS UKRAINE ‘IS NOW HOLDING THE CARDS’ AS RUSSIA SIGNALS TALKS "We think it's important to listen to those of us who live next door to Russia," Hakkarainen said. "Listen to our analysis of the situation: we consider Russia to be a long-term threat to transatlantic security — not only to Ukraine, not only to Europeans, but to transatlantic security as a whole." Finland launched the border fence initiative after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, a landmark conflict that prompted the historically neutral Nordic nation to join NATO in April 2023. Moscow has long viewed NATO’s eastward expansion as a direct security threat, using it to justify reinforcing its western defenses. When Finland officially joined the alliance, Helsinki saw an immediate reaction: over 1,300 migrants without visa arrived at its eastern border. FINLAND'S PARLIAMENT VOTES TO LIFT DECADES-OLD BAN ON NUCLEAR WEAPONS IN HISTORIC NATO DEFENSE SHIFT Finland accused Moscow of weaponizing migration as an act of "hybrid warfare," a charge the Kremlin denied. Closing the border checkpoints has proven "very effective," Hakkarainen noted. Beyond physical barriers, Finnish lawmakers passed the Border Security Act. The temporary law allows border authorities to restrict asylum applications and turn back migrants if a foreign actor attempts to destabilize the country by funneling people across the border. NATO JETS SHOOT DOWN DRONE IN LITHUANIAN AIRSPACE AS RUSSIA GROWS 'INCREASINGLY RECKLESS,' RUTTE SAYS While the law sparked some initial debate over potential human rights and international law violations, Hakkarainen emphasized that national defense took priority. "We take these concerns very seriously," he said. "But national security and our own sovereignty... weighed more heavily in this conversation, though there is broad majority support for the act." ITALY-SPAIN BORDER FEUD EXPOSES EUROPE’S DEEPENING IMMIGRATION DIVIDE "We take our security and preparedness very seriously," Hakkarainen added. articles.title: Migrant crossings to Europe by sea drop sharply amid heightened risks: IOM
articles.summary: More than 2,200 migrants died or vanished at sea in 2026, despite declining crossings into Europe, says IOM.
articles.body:
The number of migrants crossing to Europe via sea routes has dropped sharply since January this year, as the journey is becoming more dangerous, according to a new report by the International Organization for Migration (IOM).

The agency said about 60,000 migrants and refugees reached Europe by boat so far in 2026, down 39 percent from roughly 98,000 over the same period last year.

The new report shows that, despite the decline, at least 2,292 people have died or gone missing attempting the crossing, up from 1,999 over the same period last year, many on overcrowded, ill-suited boats departing Libya’s coast.

“These figures tell two stories at once,” said IOM Director General Amy Pope said Thursday.

“Fewer people are arriving by sea in Europe than at this point last year,” Pope said, noting that “people are still dying and going missing in alarming numbers trying to reach safety”.

“Behind every number is a human being, a family, a community,” she added, calling for “sustained international cooperation that saves lives, protects people on the move, combats trafficking and exploitation, and expands safe, regular pathways”.

“Nearly every death and disappearance at sea is preventable,” she said.

The toll varies by route, but the Mediterranean and Atlantic routes are “the deadliest maritime routes in the world”, according to the IOM.

Arrivals via the Central Mediterranean, the main crossing from North Africa to Italy, fell by more than half, yet deaths there still climbed from 844 to 996.

Greece recorded a smaller drop in arrivals alongside a sharp rise in deaths, from 284 to 417. Spain saw both arrivals and its overall numbers fall, though 879 people died or went missing on routes leading there.

The migration agency says the majority of people attempting to migrate are fleeing war and persecution. IOM surveys of migrants on the Central Mediterranean route found most cited economic hardship as their main reason for leaving, followed by conflict and targeted violence.

The agency has documented that more than 104,000 people have recently fled the war in Yemen, alongside large-scale displacement out of Lebanon and Syria amid the region’s ongoing conflicts.

The true death toll is almost certainly higher, IOM noted, since many boats vanish without ever being recorded.

Several European governments have pushed recently towards tougher border policies , driven in part by growing pressure from right-wing parties across the continent.

The European Union agreed in June to new rules allowing migrant deportations to countries outside the bloc. IOM is calling instead for more legal migration routes into Europe and stronger measures to reduce the risks along existing crossings.

The report follows a migration crisis that gripped Spain’s North African enclave of Ceuta in July, when more than 70,000 people crossed from Morocco over two days.

At least 90 people died en route, triggering weeks of nationwide protests over the government’s handling of the influx.

articles.title: A Chinese woman crossed the border for a concert. It could cost her family their welfare
articles.summary: A woman from a low-income family in China crossed over into Hong Kong to get to a concert she had spent months saving up for.
articles.body: A woman from a low-income family in China crossed over into Hong Kong to get to a concert she had spent months saving up for. It was a trip that Beijing’s vast surveillance apparatus didn’t miss. Now her family face the prospect of losing their government benefits for splurging on “high-end consumption.” The incident has sparked massive debate across Chinese social media over whether those receiving benefits are also entitled to small luxuries. It’s also a reminder of the staggering extent of the Chinese government’s surveillance system, one turbocharged by advances in AI and the embrace of digital payments. The story first surfaced in a post on popular site Red Note in early September by a user who said they were the young woman’s cousin. The woman, surnamed Huang, had “worked hard doing manual labor and saved up from the subsidies” to pay for the concert ticket and expenses of traveling to Hong Kong, around 235 miles (380 kilometers) from her home in Jiangxi province, the post said. That post has since been taken down, but Chinese officials have said it was indeed written by the woman’s cousin. A screenshot of it has also been used by state media reporting on the case. Hong Kong was handed back to China in 1997 following more than 100 years of British colonial rule. It is governed by separate legal and political systems to mainland China, and mainland Chinese citizens still must apply for permission to travel there. According to the Red Note post, a local social worker warned Huang before the trip that any border crossing could trigger a review of her family’s eligibility for welfare. “I can’t tell if she was actually dumb enough to think Hong Kong doesn’t count as going abroad, or if she knew perfectly well and went anyway,” it said. The family is in “extreme, extreme poverty” and the prospect of losing the payments has left them in “complete devastation,” the post said. It is unclear what concert Huang had risked so much to go and see. For many of the legions of K-Pop fans in mainland China, Hong Kong is the most accessible place to see a K-Pop concert. For the past decade, Beijing has placed an unofficial ban on performances by Korean artists on the mainland as it feuds with Seoul over trade and the presence of US weapons in South Korea. In late August in Hong Kong there was a two-day international music awards festival featuring performances from different K-Pop bands, including some famous ones such as ALLDAY PROJECT, aespa, BABYMONSTER, RIIZE, Super Junior and TOMORROW X TOGETHER. On September 7, the Social Affairs Management Bureau in Ganzhou in Jiangxi province, where the young woman lives, issued an official readout on its website in response to the heated discussion on the original Red Note post. The bureau said Huang and her family were under investigation “after she independently traveled to Hong Kong to attend a concert, the trip triggered an alert in the dynamic monitoring system for recipients of the minimum living allowance.” The city’s New Economic Development Zone’s Social Affairs Management Bureau told CNN on Wednesday that the investigation is ongoing. Over the four decades to 2020, China lifted the vast bulk of its population out of poverty, and in 2021 leader Xi Jinping declared that extreme poverty had been eliminated. But official data shows around 40 million people across the country still depend on government living subsidies. According to Ganzhou’s policy, if a household per-person income is below the minimum living allowance threshold set by the government, each person in the family could receive 1,005 yuan per month, equivalent to $150 dollars. The case has sparked so much debate that China’s state media has waded in. The Communist Party mouthpiece People’s Daily issued a commentary last week saying “of course, reasonable freedom to spend one’s money should be respected, but that freedom has limits, and people receiving public assistance are even more obligated to follow the rules.” Government basic living subsidies are “meant to cover basic necessities such as food, clothing, housing, and transportation. Going to Hong Kong to see a concert is a high-cost form of entertainment, so there is nothing unreasonable about it triggering an alert in the monitoring system,” it said. The online discussion has drawn over 120 million views on Chinese social media platform Weibo. Some commenters said they thought it would be “cruel” if the family lost their welfare. “Does being low-income mean you are not allowed to enjoy things you like?,” asked one person. But many other were less sympathetic. “Her family is struggling this badly, and she doesn’t think to use the money she earns to help her family out?” asked another user of the platform.
